title: Longest Absolute File Path
statement:
The string `input` describes a file system, one entry per line (lines are separated by `'\n'`). A line starts with some tab characters `'\t'` giving the entry's depth, followed by the entry's name: an entry at depth `d + 1` lies inside the closest line above it that has depth `d`, and depth-0 entries sit at the top level. A name that contains a dot `.` is a file (written as `name.extension`); any other name is a directory. Names are made of letters, digits and spaces (plus the dot of a file), and spaces belong to the name.

The absolute path of an entry joins the names of all directories leading to it, then its own name, with `'/'` between them (for example `"dir/subdir2/file.ext"`). Return the length of the longest absolute path that ends at a **file**, or `0` if there are no files. The input is guaranteed to describe a valid file system in which every name is non-empty.
constraints: input contains English letters, digits, spaces, '.', '\n' and '\t'
Every file and directory name has at least one character

examples.name: Example 2
input:
dir
	subdir1
		file1.ext
		subsubdir1
	subdir2
		subsubdir2
			file2.ext

tests.name: Test 7
input:
a
	b
		c
			d.e
longdirectory
	g.h

tests.name: Test 8
input:
my dir
	my file.txt
	other
		x.y

tests.name: Test 9
input:
x.y
z
	longer.txt
	deep
		deeper
			q.r

notes:
## Intuition

A brute force could, for every file, walk back up the lines to find each ancestor and build the whole path, which costs O(n²) in the worst case. But the lines arrive in depth-first order: when a line at depth `d` appears, the directories at depths `0..d-1` that contain it are exactly the most recent ones seen at those depths. Keeping one running path length per open level on a stack gives every entry's path length in O(1).

## Approach

1. Start `stack` as `[0]`: `stack[d]` is the length of the path prefix (with its trailing `/`) for entries at depth `d`. Set `best = 0`.
2. For each `line`, count the leading tabs into `depth` and take the rest as `name`.
3. Pop `stack` until it has `depth + 1` entries, closing directories that this line has left.
4. The entry's path length is `length = stack[depth] + name.length`.
5. If `name` contains a dot it is a file: update `best`. Otherwise push `length + 1` (the path plus a `/`) as the prefix for its children.
6. Return `best`.

## Example 1, step by step

Input lines: `dir`, `\tsubdir1`, `\tsubdir2`, `\t\tfile.ext`.

- `dir`: depth 0, `length = 0 + 3 = 3`, push 4, `stack = [0, 4]`.
- `subdir1`: depth 1, `length = 4 + 7 = 11`, push 12, `stack = [0, 4, 12]`.
- `subdir2`: depth 1, pop to `[0, 4]`, `length = 11`, push 12.
- `file.ext`: depth 2, `length = 12 + 8 = 20`, a file, so `best = 20`.

The answer is `20`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n) for n characters: each character is scanned a constant number of times and each push has at most one pop.
- Space: O(n) for the split lines and the stack.

## Pitfalls

- Count only tabs as depth; spaces are part of the name (`"dir\n    file.txt"` is a file named `"    file.txt"` at depth 0).
- The longest path may end at a directory; only files count.
- Several entries can sit at the top level, so do not assume one root.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `stack` | `stack[d]`: prefix length (with trailing `/`) for an entry at depth `d` |
| `best` | longest file path found so far |
| `line` | one entry of the input |
| `depth` | number of leading tabs of `line` |
| `name` | the entry's name without its tabs |
| `length` | full path length of the current entry |

narration.2: stack[d] holds the length of the path prefix, including its trailing slash, for entries at depth d.
narration.4: Handle the file system one entry (one line) at a time.
narration.6: Each leading tab adds one level of depth.
narration.9: The rest of the line is the entry's name.
narration.10: Discard prefixes of directories this line is no longer inside...
narration.11: ...until the top of the stack is this entry's parent.
narration.13: The full path is the parent's prefix plus this name.
narration.14: A dot in the name marks a file.
narration.15: Files end paths, so they are candidates for the answer.
narration.17: A directory becomes the prefix for its children, with a slash appended.
narration.20: The longest file path seen, or 0 if there was no file.
